content: Lay providers, who may include teachers, community volunteers, or traditional healers, have been shown to improve treatment success and cure rates while slightly reducing the likelihood of patients being lost to follow-up compared to self-administered therapy (SAT). However, one cohort study indicated that SAT had a higher rate of treatment completion compared to lay provider-supported treatment. Patients receiving treatment support from family members demonstrated higher treatment success rates and lower loss to follow-up compared to those using SAT. When healthcare workers provided treatment support, outcomes such as cure rates, adherence, and reduced relapse or drug resistance were better than with SAT, although SAT showed higher treatment completion rates in some cohort studies. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) care and support examined the impact of different treatment support providers. Observational studies comparing healthcare workers and lay providers found no significant differences in outcomes, though lay providers showed slightly better success rates and lower mortality, failure, and loss to follow-up. However, when family members provided treatment support, patients experienced higher mortality, loss to follow-up, and failure rates, with lower success, cure, and adherence rates compared to healthcare worker support. Thus, while treatment support by healthcare workers or trained lay providers is preferred, family member support is the least favorable option. Regarding treatment support location, randomized controlled trials and observational studies compared communityor home-based treatment support with health facility-based support. Communityor home-based support, defined as care delivered near the patient’s home or workplace, generally resulted in higher treatment success, cure, completion rates, and lower mortality and unfavorable outcomes compared to facility-based support. When compared to SAT, community/home-based support showed better adherence and lower loss to follow-up in cohort studies, though randomized trials found no significant differences. Overall, communityor home-based treatment support is preferred over facility-based support and SAT. Video-supported treatment (VST) was evaluated in two cohort studies from high-income countries, with no significant differences in treatment completion or mortality compared to in-person support. Despite limited evidence, VST offers advantages such as remote adherence monitoring, flexibility, and cost-effectiveness. It can complement or substitute in-person support for certain periods, especially in resource-limited settings where technology is increasingly accessible. VST may reduce the burden on healthcare systems and improve patient interaction at a lower cost. Combined treatment adherence interventions, including material support (e.g., food, financial incentives), psychological support, and digital tools (e.g., SMS reminders, medication monitors), were associated with higher treatment success, completion, cure, and adherence rates, as well as lower mortality and loss to follow-up. Material support, such as food or financial assistance, addresses indirect costs and improves outcomes by reducing malnutrition and enhancing immune function. Patient education and counseling also improved treatment outcomes, emphasizing the importance of culturally appropriate and targeted educational efforts. Staff education, including training and decision-making tools, improved treatment success and reduced mortality and loss to follow-up. Psychological support, such as self-help groups or counseling, was linked to better treatment completion and cure rates, though concerns about confounding factors and non-randomized allocation were noted. Targeting marginalized populations with psychological support can enhance health equity. For multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), ambulatory care and decentralized models are recommended over hospitalization. Decentralized care, provided in local communities by healthcare workers or trained laypersons, is practical for scaling up MDR-TB treatment. Observational studies suggest that decentralized care does not compromise treatment quality and may be more cost-effective and accessible. In summary, treatment support is most effective when delivered at home or in the community by healthcare workers or trained lay providers. Material and psychological support, patient education, and digital tools further enhance adherence and outcomes. Decentralized and ambulatory care models are preferred for MDR-TB, with a focus on patient-centered approaches and equitable access to resources.
